name: Film or Series Project Pitch Deck
description: A cinematic noir pitch system for presenting a screen project's logline, world, characters, narrative arc, visual language, audience, distribution path, team, budget, and financing ask.
style_guide:
# Film or Series Project Pitch Deck

## Design intent

Create a cinematic, producer-ready pitch for a feature, limited series, returning series, documentary, or other screen project. The visual language is prestige noir: near-black blue canvas, sodium-gold emphasis, cold cyan atmosphere, bone-white type, restrained editorial italics, widescreen imagery, production-style metadata, and a clear progression from creative promise to market and financing logic.

The deck should help a producer, studio, streamer, financier, broadcaster, or sales partner understand the project without confusing mood with evidence. The reference previews are visual-language examples only. Do not copy their title, logline, story, characters, world, images, comparables, format, budget, schedule, talent, audience, distribution plan, ask, or contact details.

## Canvas and grid

- Use a fixed `1280 × 720 px` 16:9 canvas with `30–42 px` side margins, a `22–30 px` reel-style header, and a `20–26 px` footer for rights, draft, and source status.
- Use a 12-column grid with `14–18 px` gutters. Align logline boxes, project-vital cards, character portraits, story beats, moodboard frames, palette bars, audience circles, market charts, windows, team cards, and budget lines.
- Reserve `82–115 px` for section cue, headline, and one supporting statement. Let one creative or commercial exhibit dominate each page.
- Prefer cinematic full-bleed covers, `8/4` pitch-and-vitals splits, three-character rows, `7/5` moodboard-and-craft layouts, and wide budget or distribution structures.
- Use `16–22 px` between large modules and `8–13 px` within cards. Maintain a clear left-to-right reading path even on dense pages.
- Keep analytical pages consistently dark and use image frames with enough tonal separation for captions to remain readable.

## Color system

### Core palette

- Projection black: `#070C11`. Use for the main canvas and deepest image overlays.
- Slate midnight: `#17212B`. Use for cards, table rows, comparison panels, and elevated surfaces.
- Sodium gold: `#D5A04A`. Use for title accents, section rules, pivotal story beats, active distribution windows, key budget values, and the ask.
- Cold cyan: `#4F8FA3`. Use for technological, nocturnal, institutional, or secondary analytical cues and one alternate chart series.
- Bone white: `#EDE2CA`. Use for headlines, logline, core values, and readable body copy.
- Smoke gray: `#87919A`. Use for secondary descriptions, inactive phases, metadata, and sources.
- Warning ember: `#B95A32`. Use only for a genuine production, financing, schedule, or rights risk.

### Semantic use

- Gold signals narrative or decision priority; it does not by itself imply award potential, market value, or attachment.
- Cyan signals atmosphere, technology, secondary state, or comparison. Keep its role stable across the deck.
- Bone white is the main reading color and should not be replaced with dim gray for long passages.
- Preserve the source imagery's intended grade. Do not recolor character or location imagery until important story or identity information is lost.

## Typography

- Use `Inter`, `Aptos`, `Helvetica Neue`, or a similarly strong cinematic sans-serif.
- Use a restrained italic for logline, tonal phrase, creator statement, or one phrase in a headline. Avoid decorative screenplay fonts.
- Use `IBM Plex Mono`, `Roboto Mono`, or another mono face for draft numbers, reel codes, formats, runtimes, dates, legal notes, scene references, and source labels.
- Cover title: `58–76 px`, bold or extended. Page headline: `31–40 px`, bold. Section cue: `9–11 px`, uppercase, tracked. Logline: `20–27 px`, italic. Body: `14–17 px`. Tables and credits: `10–13 px`. Rights footer: `8–10 px`.
- Use tabular numerals for episode count, runtime, schedule, budget, market data, and financing.
- Keep paragraphs short. The deck should read like a confident visual treatment, not a screenplay excerpt.

## Components

- Cards use dark slate fills, `1 px` gold or blue-gray borders, small corners, and no shadows.
- Project-vital cards should show format, genre, language, episode or runtime, stage, budget range, rights status, and target schedule only when confirmed.
- Character cards pair a consistent portrait crop with role, dramatic need, conflict, relationship, and arc—not a full biography.
- Story-beat rails show episode or act, turning point, consequence, and unresolved drive.
- Comparable-title tables must explain the relevant shared dimension and the meaningful difference.
- Team cards distinguish confirmed, attached, in discussion, contingent, and open roles.
- Budget tables should show major cost categories, currency, basis, contingency, and whether values are preliminary or approved.

## Charts and diagrams

- Favor logline and positioning boxes, character and arc maps, episode or act rails, moodboard grids, palette strips, craft-principle lists, comparable-title tables, audience structures, market bars, release-window timelines, team matrices, and budget allocations.
- Story diagrams should reveal causality, escalation, character change, and season or feature resolution without giving every plot detail equal weight.
- Market and audience views need format, genre, territory, release window, platform, and source consistency.
- Distribution paths should distinguish festival, market, broadcast, theatrical, streamer, international sales, franchise, and ancillary rights as applicable.
- Budget views should connect scope to schedule, locations, cast, VFX, post, contingency, bond, insurance, and delivery requirements.
- Avoid 3D charts, decorative film reels, fake clapperboards, and unstructured moodboard collages.

## Composition families

### Cinematic cover

Use one rights-cleared or project-owned hero frame with a strong black gradient. Place the title, format, one restrained tagline or tonal statement, presenter, production entity, date, and draft status without crowding the image.

### Logline and positioning

Use one prominent logline box, a concise positioning statement, project-vital cards, core themes, and a short why-now rationale. Keep aspirational language separate from confirmed facts.

### World, characters, and narrative arc

Introduce the world in one precise paragraph, then use a row of central characters and a compact act, episode, or season spine. Prioritize dramatic function and change.

### Visual tone and comparables

Use four or fewer tonal frames with captions describing light, lens, texture, production design, or sound. Pair them with a palette, craft rules, and a focused comparable-title table.

### Audience, market, and distribution

Show primary and adjacent audiences, relevant market evidence, and a phased distribution or windowing plan. Do not infer market size directly from a broad genre audience.

### Creative team, budget, and ask

Use role-based team cards, a high-level production budget, financing context, and one precise partner request. State attachment and rights status visibly.

## Imagery

- Use project-owned stills, concept art, location photography, production design, wardrobe, prop, lens or lighting tests, storyboards, and licensed mood references.
- Label images as project still, concept, mood reference, target, location, test, or generated visualization. Mood references are not cast or production commitments.
- Keep a consistent cinematic aspect ratio and grade within each image family. Crop for narrative information rather than decorative faces.
- Credit sources and rights status. Do not include identifiable talent, trademarks, private locations, or copyrighted frames without an appropriate basis.
- Avoid generic red-carpet imagery, fake festival laurels, fake platform logos, clapperboard stock photos, AI faces presented as attached cast, and unrelated cinematic cityscapes.

## Content integrity

- Do not invent rights ownership, chain of title, attachments, cast, director, producer, financing, budget, tax incentives, distribution interest, comparable performance, market size, audience, schedule, locations, episode count, or release date.
- Clearly distinguish attached, offer out, in discussion, desired, and illustrative talent or partners.
- Market data must specify title, format, platform, territory, release date, measurement, source, and comparability limitation.
- Budget figures need currency, date, stage, assumptions, exclusions, contingency, incentives, financing status, and per-episode or total basis.
- Distribution plans should be labeled as strategy, target, discussion, commitment, or confirmed agreement.
- Confirm underlying rights, life rights, adaptation rights, music, archive, artwork, likeness, and location permissions where relevant.
- If evidence is missing, omit it or label it `concept`, `mood reference`, `target`, `estimate`, `preliminary`, `in discussion`, or `to be confirmed`. Never fabricate an attachment or market claim.

## Avoid

- Do not copy preview title, premise, world, characters, imagery, plot, themes, craft language, comparables, data, team, budget, distribution, ask, or contacts.
- Do not use mood references as if they were owned production stills or attached talent.
- Do not claim a project is the next successful title based on superficial tonal similarity.
- Do not let cinematic atmosphere hide unclear format, rights, budget, schedule, audience, or partner need.
- Do not use gold on every heading and border; scarcity creates the prestige tone.
- Do not use glossy gradients, glass cards, large rounded corners, heavy glow, fake film grain over text, 3D charts, or unreadable legal footers.
- Do not show an unsupported budget as precise, a target window as booked, or a creative wish as a commitment.
